docs.title: Nolain Data Query
docs.text:
Nolain answers questions about a file that already lives on your computer. You type something like “What is total revenue by country?”, and you get a table — and, if you asked for one, a chart — computed from that file.

The unusual part is where the work happens. Your file never leaves your machine. A remote service sees only a sketch of the data: column names, types, a few sample rows. It returns a recipe — executable analysis, and optionally a computation graph and a chart contract. Your computer runs that recipe against the real file. The numbers you see are true because they were computed locally, not because a model claimed them.

This folder is the book for that system. It assumes you have never opened the repository.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
Three kinds of reader, one narrative:

  • You want to use Nolain. Create an account, paste an API key, ask a question. Start with Using Nolain, then Credits. You can stop there.
  • You want to understand how it works before you change anything. After the user chapters, read How Nolain is built, then The parts of the system, then A conversation from start to finish.
  • You want to run, extend, or operate it. Continue through Signing in, the Cloud API, and Operations.

If you only have twenty minutes: this page, Using Nolain, and the first half of How Nolain is built.

docs.title: How the book is organized
docs.text:
Each chapter assumes you have not yet seen the next one. Terms are introduced when they are needed, then reused. When a concept has a name in the codebase, the chapter explains the idea first and mentions the implementing type in parentheses afterward.

The chapters follow a single arc: what the product is, why it is shaped this way, how a question travels through it, and only then how to call, run, and operate it.

docs.title: A few words you will meet again
docs.text:
You do not need these yet. They are here so later chapters can use them without stopping to define them twice.

Word Meaning in this book Sketch A compact description of a local file: columns, types, summaries, sample values. This is all the cloud is allowed to see. Artifact Something the cloud produces for the desktop to use: executable analysis, an optional computation graph, an optional chart contract. Capability A product the cloud knows how to generate. Today there is one: descriptive analysis of a single file. Plan An engine for a Capability — the sequence of steps that produces artifacts. Today the implemented engine is Pandas. Intent What kind of conversational turn this is (answer from the sketch, refuse, ask a clarifying question, or generate analysis). Not a product. Credits The unit you pay in. Each call to a language model settles immediately.

docs.title: Trying it on your machine
docs.text:
From the repository root, install dependencies:

./setup.sh

You will need two terminals. Before the first one, set the environment variables in Running the Cloud API yourself.

  1. Start Redis, the Cloud API, and the background worker:

bash ./scripts/launch-cloud-dev.sh

  1. Start the local engine and the desktop app:

bash ./launch.sh

The Cloud API listens at http://127.0.0.1:8000. The local engine listens at http://127.0.0.1:8001.

For packaged builds, see distribute.sh (Linux) and distribute-windows.ps1 (Windows) in the repository root.

The next chapter is Using Nolain: how a person goes from “I have a file” to “I have an answer.”

docs.title: Using Nolain
docs.text:
This chapter is for someone who wants to ask questions about a local file. It covers four steps: create an account, generate an API key, paste that key into the desktop app, and ask a question. The chapters after this one explain credits, then how the system is built. You do not need those to get an answer.

Nolain is a desktop application plus a Cloud API. The desktop app reads your file, sends a sketch of it to the cloud, and runs whatever recipe comes back. The Cloud API is the remote reasoning service: it turns your question and that sketch into executable analysis. Your rows never leave the machine.

docs.title: 1. Create an account
docs.text:
1. Open the Nolain portal.
  2. Click Sign Up and create an account with your email.
  3. Verify the email.

The portal is the account desk: it is where you sign in, manage keys, and see your credit balance. The desktop app does not create accounts; it uses a key you bring from the portal.

docs.title: 2. Generate an API key
docs.text:
Think of the key as a library card. Anyone who holds it can spend the credits on your account.

  1. Log in to the portal.
  2. Go to Dashboard → API Keys.
  3. Click Generate New Key.
  4. Copy the key. It is shown once. Store it somewhere safe — a password manager is enough.

A key looks like this:

sk-free-3f9a1c72b4de5e01

docs.title: 3. Enter the key in the desktop app
docs.text:
1. Open Nolain Data Query.
  2. In the Left Sidebar, click Settings.
  3. Paste the key into the API Key field.
  4. Click Save. The app validates the key and shows your plan and remaining credits.

The key is stored on your machine. The only place it is sent is the Nolain Cloud API, when you make a request.

docs.title: 4. Ask a question
docs.text:
1. In the Left Sidebar, choose a local file (.parquet or .csv).
  2. Open Ask Queries and type a question in ordinary language, for example:

What is the total revenue by country?

  1. Press Enter (or click Execute).
  2. Results appear in the table. If you asked for a chart, it appears as well.

What just happened, in one paragraph: the desktop derived a sketch of the file (column names, types, a few samples) and sent that sketch with your question. The cloud decided this was a real analysis request, produced Pandas code — and, if your toggles were on, a computation graph and a chart contract — and sent those artifacts back. The desktop ran them against the file still sitting on disk. How Nolain is built tells that story in full.

Not every question goes through that pipeline. “What columns do I have?” can be answered from the sketch alone. “What’s the weather in Oslo?” is off-topic and gets a short refusal. Those branches exist so you are not charged for work the product cannot do.

docs.title: Plan limits
docs.text:
Credits are the unit of payment. They reset at the start of each UTC calendar month. Credits explains the formula; the table below is the allowance.

Plan Credits / month Price Free 1,000 Free Premium 50,000 See the portal

When the balance reaches zero, you will see a message like:

No credits remaining on your account. Subscribe or top up at the portal to continue using the Cloud API.

To add credits, open Account → Subscription or Top Up on the portal.

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.text:
Can I have several API keys? Yes. Generate as many as you need from the portal. They all spend the same account balance.

What if I lose a key? On the portal, deactivate the old key and generate a new one. Paste the new key into desktop Settings.

Is my data sent to the cloud? No. Only the sketch (column names, types, summaries, sample values) and your question are sent. The file stays on your machine.

Why did I get a refusal instead of a table? Nolain’s enabled product is descriptive analysis of one file — aggregations, comparisons, rankings, trends, quality checks, reshape, optional charts. It will not forecast, run statistical inference, optimize, or detect anomalies until those products are added. A refusal is the system being honest about that boundary.

The next chapter, Credits, is what those 1,000 (or 50,000) credits actually buy, and why a “simple question” is not always one charge.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
The last chapter got you to a working query. This one answers a practical question: what does a question cost?

Credits are prepaid tokens for reasoning work — calls to a language model. They are not a charge for “running your data.” Local execution on your machine is free. You pay for the thinking the cloud does on your behalf.

Technical charging, ledgers, and HTTP 402 behavior live in Billing internals. This chapter stays on the user side: the unit, the monthly allowance, a worked example, and what is free.

docs.title: What a credit is
docs.text:
1,000 credits = $1 of model usage, or 1 credit = $0.001.

Two numbers are added together on every model call:

  • Token credits — the model’s actual token cost, converted at that rate and rounded up.
  • Surplus credits — a platform margin, a configurable fraction of token credits. The default is 100%, so the surplus equals the token credits.

With the default surplus, the amount deducted is roughly twice the raw token cost. Surplus exists so retries, pricing drift, and the cost of running the service are not hidden inside a flat “per question” price.

docs.title: Why not charge per question?
docs.text:
A question is not one call. The cloud may classify your intent, read the wording for ambiguities, generate analysis code, optionally compile a computation graph, optionally write a chart contract, and — if you ask — frame the result as a short narrative. Each of those is a separate model call. A failed compile still used a model. A clarification still used a model.

Charging per call matches what actually happened. The product is honest that a “simple question” can be several calls, and that a question which never generates code can still cost something if a model was asked to classify it.

docs.title: How much you start with each month
docs.text:
Credits reset on the UTC calendar month. Top-ups you purchase do not expire at month end.

Plan Credits at the start of each month Approx. dollar value Free 1,000 $1 Premium 50,000 $50 Top-ups Added when purchased do not expire at month end

Your balance appears in the desktop Settings panel and on the portal.

docs.title: How one model call is priced
docs.text:
token_credits   = ceil(model_cost_usd × 1000)
surplus_credits = ceil(token_credits × surplus_rate)    # default surplus_rate = 1.0
charged_credits = token_credits + surplus_credits

Example: a call that cost $0.0026 in tokens becomes 3 token credits (ceil(2.6)). With 100% surplus that is another 3, so 6 credits are deducted.

Part Meaning Token credits Actual model usage (1 credit ≈ $0.001 of tokens), rounded up Surplus credits Platform margin as a fraction of token credits (default 100%)

Every model call is charged as soon as it completes. Failed or cancelled jobs still cost credits for calls already made. Queueing a job, by itself, does not.

docs.title: What a full question tends to cost
docs.text:
The benchmark report ran 50 hard retail questions through the desktop conversation loop. Those totals include every worker model call in the job. They do not include the cheaper conversation-side calls (classification, semantic reading, optional narrative), so a live question can cost a little more than the figures below.

Setup Average credits per question GPT-5.6 Luna, analysis code only 4.08 DeepSeek V4 Flash, analysis code only 2.76 GPT-5.6 Luna, analysis code plus computation graph 38.84

On the Free plan (1,000 credits/month), those averages imply roughly:

  • ~245 GPT-5.6 Luna analysis-only answers, or
  • ~26 GPT-5.6 Luna answers that also built a graph, or
  • a different amount depending on the model, the question, and retries

Premium (50,000 credits/month) is 50× the Free allowance. These are measured slices, not a guaranteed number of questions. Turning on the computation graph is the largest cost lever in that sample: the same model went from about 4 credits to about 39.

A successful job’s running total appears as billing.charged_credits on the job status the desktop polls.

docs.title: What is free, and what is not
docs.text:
Free

  • Replies that never call a model (some metadata answers: column lists, row counts, types)
  • Reading the status of a job that already started

Not free

  • Any step that invokes a model: classifying the turn, reading the question for ambiguity, generating code, compiling a graph, writing a chart contract, framing a narrative

Off-topic questions still cost the classification call if a model was used to decide they were off-topic.

docs.title: Buying more credits
docs.text: Premium plans and top-up packs are sold through Stripe. Purchased credits are added to your balance after payment.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
This chapter is for someone standing up the portal: the website where a person creates an account, signs in with Google, and manages API keys. The desktop app does not create accounts. It uses a key the portal issued. The Cloud API does not talk to Google directly. It trusts tokens that Supabase issued after Google sign-in.

If you only want to use an existing portal, you do not need this chapter. Using Nolain is enough. If you want the Cloud API running without Google at all, a developer key in Running the Cloud API yourself is enough. Come here when you need the three-party handshake to work.

The rest of the chapter is the how: create a Supabase project, create a Google OAuth client, point them at each other, tell the Cloud API and the website the right URLs, and verify end-to-end.

docs.title: What the handshake is
docs.text:
Four pieces share the job, and each is allowed to see only its part.

Piece Job Google Proves the person owns a Google account Supabase Auth Turns that proof into a session token, and stores a profile row The portal website Login page and account dashboard. Holds the public Supabase key, never the service-role secret The Cloud API Validates the session token, creates and revokes API keys, reads the credit balance

The path a person actually takes:

  1. They click Continue with Google on /login.
  2. Google sends them to Supabase, Supabase sends them to /account.
  3. The website calls the Cloud API with Authorization: Bearer <access_token>.
  4. The API checks that token with Supabase and reads or writes keys in clients_nolain_query.

Two redirect URIs, two different jobs. Google only needs to know the Supabase callback (https://<project>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback). Supabase only needs to know your site (/account). Putting the website URL in Google’s console, or the Google client id in the Cloud API .env, is the usual way this goes wrong.

The click-by-click work starts with a database. Supabase holds profiles, API keys, and credit balances. Google only proves identity; it never sees those tables.

docs.title: 1.1 Create or open a project
docs.text:
1. Go to Supabase dashboard.
  2. Create a new project (or use your existing one for the Cloud API).
  3. Wait for the database to finish provisioning.

docs.title: 1.2 Run database migrations
docs.text:
In SQL Editor, run these files in order:

  1. cloud_api/sql/001_create_clients.sql (if not already applied)
  2. cloud_api/sql/002_auth_users.sql
  3. cloud_api/sql/003_account_balance.sql

This creates:

  • public.profiles_nolain_query — one row per auth user, including credit_balance
  • clients_nolain_query.user_id — links API keys to users
  • credit_balance_ledger_nolain_query and credit RPCs
  • A trigger that auto-creates a profile on sign-up

docs.title: 1.3 Copy API credentials
docs.text:
Go to Project Settings → API and note:

Setting Used by Project URL Cloud API + website anon public key Website only (safe in browser) service_role secret Cloud API only (never expose)

docs.title: 2. Google Cloud Console (OAuth)
docs.text: Google Sign-In for Supabase requires a Web application OAuth client created in the Google Cloud Console. Google does not expose this client type via gcloud or REST API — the Console UI is the only supported path (API-created clients are IAP-only and will not work with Supabase).

docs.title: Quick path: run the helper script
docs.text:
From the repo root (requires a browser on your machine):

# Refresh gcloud first if you use it for project detection:
gcloud auth login

# Opens the right Console + Supabase pages and prints your redirect URI:
./cloud_api/scripts/setup-google-oauth.sh

# Or pin a specific GCP project:
GCP_PROJECT=nolainquery ./cloud_api/scripts/setup-google-oauth.sh

The script reads SUPABASE_URL from cloud_api/.env and prints the exact redirect URI:

https://<your-supabase-ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback

docs.title: Manual path: detailed click-by-click guide
docs.text: Use this if you prefer the Console directly, or the script cannot open your browser.

docs.title: 2.1 Choose or create a Google Cloud project
docs.text:
1. Open Google Cloud Console.
  2. Click the project picker (top bar, next to "Google Cloud").
  3. Either:
  4. Use an existing project — select it from the list, or
  5. Create new → New project → Name: nolainquery → Create → wait ~30 s → select it.

Keep this project dedicated to nolainquery auth if possible. Do not reuse a throwaway/training project unless you are okay sharing its OAuth consent screen.

docs.title: 2.2 Configure the OAuth consent screen (first time only)
docs.text:
1. In the left sidebar, open Google Auth Platform (or search "OAuth consent screen").
  2. Direct link (replace YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID): https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/overview?project=YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID
  3. If you see "Google Auth Platform not configured yet", click Get started.
  4. App information screen: | Field | Value | |---|---| | App name | nolainquery | | User support email | Your email (e.g. the Gmail you sign in with) | | App logo | Optional — skip for now |
  5. Click Next.
  6. Audience screen:
  7. Select External (allows any Google account to sign in).
  8. Click Next.
  9. Contact information screen:
  10. Developer contact email: your email.
  11. Click Next.
  12. Finish screen:
  13. Review the summary → click Create (or Continue to dashboard).
  14. Scopes (if prompted separately):
  15. Click Add or remove scopes.
  16. Ensure these are included (they are usually added by default):
    • .../auth/userinfo.email
    • .../auth/userinfo.profile
    • openid
  17. Click Update → Save.

docs.title: 2.3 Add test users (required while app is in "Testing")
docs.text:
While the publishing status is Testing, only listed test users can sign in.

  1. In Google Auth Platform, go to Audience (left sidebar).
  2. Under Test users, click Add users.
  3. Add the Gmail address(es) you will use to test login.
  4. Click Save.

When you go to production, change publishing status to In production under Audience → Publishing status → Publish app (Google may require verification if you request sensitive scopes — email/profile/openid do not require it).

docs.title: 2.4 Create the OAuth Web client
docs.text:
1. In Google Auth Platform, open Clients (left sidebar).
  2. Direct link: https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/clients/create?project=YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID
  3. Click Create client (or + Create client).
  4. Fill in the form:
Field Value Application type Web application Name nolainquery portal

  1. Authorized JavaScript origins — leave empty. Supabase handles the OAuth flow server-side; you do not need your website origin here.

  2. Authorized redirect URIs — click + Add URI and paste exactly:

https://<YOUR-SUPABASE-REF>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback

Find <YOUR-SUPABASE-REF> in Supabase → Project Settings → General → Reference ID, or from your SUPABASE_URL (the subdomain before .supabase.co).

Example:

https://fihkvacuiguhrhlnjscr.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback

Common mistakes: - Trailing slash (/callback/ vs /callback) — must match exactly, no trailing slash. - Using http:// — must be https://. - Putting http://localhost:5173/account here — that URI goes in Supabase, not Google.

  1. Click Create.
  2. A dialog shows Client ID and Client secret.
  3. Copy both immediately — you need them for Supabase (next section).
  4. Click Download JSON optionally as backup (store securely, never commit to git).

docs.title: 2.5 What you should have now
docs.text:
Item Example shape Used in Client ID 123456789-abc.apps.googleusercontent.com Supabase Google provider Client secret GOCSPX-... Supabase Google provider Redirect URI https://xxx.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback Google Console only

You do not add these to cloud_api/.env. The Cloud API validates Supabase JWTs, not Google tokens directly.

docs.title: 3. Enable Google provider in Supabase
docs.text:
1. Open your Supabase project dashboard.
  2. Direct link (replace ref): https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<YOUR-SUPABASE-REF>/auth/providers
  3. Click Google in the provider list.
  4. Toggle Enable Sign in with Google to ON.
  5. Paste from Google Console (step 2.4):
  6. Client ID → 123456789-....apps.googleusercontent.com
  7. Client Secret → GOCSPX-...
  8. Leave Skip nonce check off unless Supabase docs instruct otherwise for your setup.
  9. Click Save.

docs.title: 3.1 Redirect URLs (Supabase)
docs.text:
Go to Authentication → URL Configuration (https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<REF>/auth/url-configuration):

Setting Local dev Production Site URL http://localhost:5173 https://nolain.app Redirect URLs http://localhost:5173/account https://nolain.app/account

Click Add URL for each redirect. Supabase allows multiple entries — add both local and prod.

How redirects work: Google → Supabase callback (…/auth/v1/callback) → your site (/account). That is why Google only needs the Supabase URI, and Supabase needs your site URIs.

docs.title: 4. Cloud API environment
docs.text:
Edit cloud_api/.env:

# Existing
SUPABASE_URL=https://YOUR-PROJECT-REF.supabase.co
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=eyJhbGciOi...

# Portal CORS — comma-separated browser origins
CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173,http://127.0.0.1:5173,https://nolain.app

Restart the API after changes.

docs.title: Auth endpoints
docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /api/auth/me Profile + API keys + usage summary GET /api/auth/keys List active keys (masked) POST /api/auth/keys Create a free-tier key (full key returned once) DELETE /api/auth/keys/{id} Revoke (deactivate) a key

All require: Authorization: Bearer <supabase_access_token>

docs.title: 5. Website environment
docs.text:
Create nolainquery-website/.env:

VITE_SUPABASE_URL=https://YOUR-PROJECT-REF.supabase.co
VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=eyJhbGciOi...   # anon public key only
VITE_CLOUD_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000

For production (Vercel, etc.), set the same variables in your host's environment panel. Use your deployed API URL for VITE_CLOUD_API_URL.

Start the website:

cd nolainquery-website
npm install
npm run dev

docs.title: 6. Verify end-to-end
docs.text:
1. Start Cloud API: ./scripts/launch-cloud-dev.sh
  2. Start website: npm run dev in nolainquery-website/
  3. Open http://localhost:5173/login
  4. Sign in with Google → you should land on /account
  5. Click Create key → copy the key
  6. Test the key against the API:
curl -H "X-API-Key: sk-free-..." http://127.0.0.1:8000/health

docs.title: 7. Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Run 002_auth_users.sql on production Supabase
  • [ ] Google OAuth redirect URI uses production Supabase project ref
  • [ ] Supabase Site URL and Redirect URLs include https://nolain.app/account
  • [ ] CORS_ORIGINS includes https://nolain.app
  • [ ] VITE_CLOUD_API_URL points to your production API
  • [ ] Never commit .env files or expose SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause Google sign-in fails immediately Wrong Client ID/Secret in Supabase, or redirect URI missing/mismatched in Google Console redirect_uri_mismatch from Google Redirect URI in Google must be exactly https://<ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback (no trailing slash) Access blocked: app has not completed verification Add your Gmail under Google Auth Platform → Audience → Test users (app is in Testing mode) Error 403: org_internal You chose Internal audience — switch to External, or use a Workspace account Redirect loop or "invalid redirect" Add /account URL to Supabase Redirect URLs API returns 401 on /api/auth/me Expired token — sign out and back in; check service role key CORS error in browser Add your website origin to CORS_ORIGINS and restart API Profile not created Run 002_auth_users.sql; check trigger on_auth_user_created_nolain_query exists "Database error" on key create Run 001_create_clients.sql first; confirm clients_nolain_query.user_id column exists

The click-by-click work is done. For the Cloud API’s own environment and the owner developer key, continue with Running the Cloud API yourself. For what those keys spend, see Credits (users) and Billing internals (operators).

docs.title: A conversation from start to finish
docs.text:
The last two chapters explained the design and named the parts. This chapter is the desktop product in motion: what happens, request by request, from the moment you load a file to the moment a table (and maybe a chart) appears.

The path described here is Ask Queries. There is a second door — direct generation without a chat — that covers only the middle of this story (produce artifacts, poll, execute). It does not classify, clarify, or repair. Both doors produce the same Capability. This chapter is the full loop.

You will see HTTP paths. They are the messages on the wire, not the entry point for the ideas. The ideas are: open a session on a sketch, decide what kind of turn this is, maybe generate, execute locally, report back, repair if needed, optionally narrate.

docs.title: The loop at a glance
docs.text:
Seven moves. The rest of the chapter walks each one, then shows what changes if the question is off-topic, ambiguous, or fails on the real file.

  1. Start a session with the current sketch. No model call, no charge.
  2. Send the question (and your graph/chart toggles). The server classifies the turn and either replies immediately or admits a generation job.
  3. Poll the job until artifacts are ready (or the job fails).
  4. Execute locally on the engine that has the file.
  5. Report the outcome. On success, the result is stored for follow-ups. On failure with budget remaining, the server queues a repair.
  6. If repairing, poll and execute again until the run succeeds or the budget is exhausted.
  7. Optionally ask for a narrative wrapping of the numbers.

Two kinds of Pandas retry share a chain-wide ceiling (default 9 generate-or- repair calls) but spend different source budgets:

Kind When Where it happens Sandbox retry Truncated, empty, or statically illegal code during cloud generation Inside the worker, before anything ships Runtime repair Code passed those checks but failed when executed locally After you report the error; a new job, no new classification

Compiler and chart retries are a third budget and are not spent here.

docs.title: What you need before the first message
docs.text:
• The desktop has asked the local engine for a sketch (POST http://localhost:8001/data_summary).
  • Requests carry a valid API key (X-API-Key).
  • Sessions are reused until the desktop resets local state. On the server they expire after 24 hours.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
Suppose the loaded file has columns Invoice, Quantity, Price, Country, and you ask:

What are the top 5 countries by total revenue?

You have left both toggles on: compile a computation graph, and produce a chart.

docs.title: 1. Start a session
docs.text: The desktop posts the sketch and receives a session_id. Nothing is classified. Nothing is charged. Redis now holds conversation:{session_id} — a short-lived thread bound to that sketch.

docs.title: 2. Send the question
docs.text:
The desktop posts the session id, the question, the sketch, and the toggles. Without a clarification payload, the conversation graph runs:

  1. Classify the turn (one model call). For this question the kind is a data question.
  2. Read the wording for ambiguities (semantic analysis). “Revenue” might mean Quantity * Price, or it might mean something else in your file. If the reading is ambiguous, you get a clarification and the loop waits. If it fails, you get a text reply and no job.
  3. If the reading is clear, policy admits the Pandas Plan with your toggles and queues a worker job.

The response type tells the desktop what to do next:

Response type Meaning What the desktop does text_response Off-topic, unsafe, underspecified, explanation, out of scope, or fallback Show the text meta_answer Question about the file’s structure Show the metadata answer clarification Ambiguous terms Resend with your chosen interpretations generation Job accepted Poll task_id

A generation response also echoes capability_id, plan_id, and the toggles the server actually admitted, so the desktop can show what was queued.

Clarification shortcut. When you resend with clarifications filled in, classification and semantic reading are skipped. The meaning of the question is treated as settled; the server queues the Plan with the current toggles.

What the classifier is allowed to do. It chooses the kind of turn. For generation kinds it may suggest a Capability and a Plan from the live catalog. It does not turn the graph or the chart on or off. Those are your toggles. Policy, not the prompt, rebuilds the pipeline.

docs.title: 3. Poll the job
docs.text:
The desktop asks for status about every 1.5 seconds. When the pipeline status is success or failed, the job is done.

The payload that matters for the rest of the loop:

  • pandas_code — the program to run locally
  • optional graph and visualization_spec — if you asked for them and those stations succeeded
  • pandas_retries_left — remaining local repair jobs
  • pandas_sandbox_retries_left — remaining in-cloud static retries
  • pandas_attempts_used / pandas_total_max_attempts — chain-wide usage and ceiling
  • billing.charged_credits — running total for worker model calls
  • generation_attempts — per-call diagnostics (finish reason, selected repair profile, tokens, accepted or rejected)

While the job runs, the worker may retry writing the code internally (truncated completion, empty extract, static sandbox reject). Partial length-limited code is never sent for execution.

docs.title: 4. Execute locally
docs.text:
Execution is on the local engine (port 8001), never on the Cloud API:

  • run the Pandas code against the loaded file
  • if a graph artifact is present, run that too

No cloud credit is charged for this step. This is the first moment the analysis meets the rows.

docs.title: 5. Report the outcome
docs.text:
After every local run — success or failure — the desktop tells the conversation what happened, so follow-up questions have execution context.

Success. The server stores the result and returns { "status": "ok" }. Later, “how did you calculate that?” can be answered from this memory without generating again.

Failure with budget remaining. If the error and the failed code are both present, the previous job succeeded on the cloud side (it shipped code), and pandas_retries_left is still positive, the server:

  1. Reads the remaining budget from that job
  2. Queues a new generate-and-repair job with the failed code and the error (no new classifier, no new semantic turn)
  3. Decrements the runtime-repair budget on the new job
  4. Resets the in-cloud sandbox budget for that repair (so a depleted sandbox count cannot block a new attempt) and carries the chain-wide attempt count forward (so repairs cannot multiply forever)
  5. Returns { "status": "repairing", "task_id": "..." }

The desktop then repeats poll → execute → report with the new task id. If no retries remain, the server returns { "status": "ok" } and the desktop keeps the error.

Repair settings are chosen from the kind of failure and the retry index (syntax vs runtime vs truncation, first try vs repeated signature). All Pandas generate-or-repair calls remain bounded by the chain-wide ceiling.

docs.title: 6. Optional narrative
docs.text: After a successful execution, the desktop may ask the cloud to frame the numbers as a short paragraph. That is another model call, charged if it runs. If it fails, the endpoint still returns an empty narrative: you keep the table.

docs.title: The same loop, other kinds of turn
docs.text:
The revenue question was the happy path. Dialogue exists so that not every message takes it.

What you asked What the server does Credits “What’s the weather?” / jailbreak / “analyze my data” Classify → text reply Charged if that path called a model “What columns do I have?” Classify → answer from the sketch Free when no model is called “How did you calculate that?” Classify → grounded text from stored result Charged if that path called a model “Forecast next quarter’s sales” Classify or safety net → named refusal Charged if that path called a model Clear data question Classify → semantic reading → generation Per model call in the job Ambiguous data question Classify → semantic reading → clarification Per model call already made Your reply to a clarification Skip classify/semantic → generation Per model call in the job “That doesn’t look right” Always semantic reading → generation Per model call in the job Local Pandas error, retries left Report → repair job Per model call in the repair job Local execution Desktop port 8001 No cloud charge Answer framing Optional synthesize Per model call

Worker cost details and Plan station lists: The parts of the system.

docs.title: What the product will and will not do
docs.text:
• Data questions — including charts and reshape — admit the Pandas Plan. Charts set the visualization toggle; they do not change which Plan you are on.
  • Requests no registered Capability can serve return a text message naming what is available, and do not admit generation. A wording-based safety net still catches forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection while only descriptive analysis is enabled.
  • Explanation requests use saved result context and do not queue generation.

docs.title: The HTTP surface, as a table
docs.text:
Once the story is clear, the endpoints are just names for the moves:

Endpoint Move POST /api/v1/conversation/start Open a session on a sketch POST /api/v1/conversation/message Classify (or skip) and maybe admit a job GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} Poll generation POST /api/v1/conversation/result Store the local outcome; maybe queue repair POST /api/v1/conversation/synthesize Optional narrative GET /api/v1/conversation/{session_id} Read the session DELETE /api/v1/conversation/{session_id} Delete the session POST /api/v1/cancel_task/{task_id} Cooperative cancel between stages

Session read and delete currently do not verify that the calling key created the session. Cancellation does: only the key that owns the job may cancel it. Model calls already completed keep their charges.

Request bodies, response shapes, and curl examples: Calling the Cloud API. Job diagnostics, attempt logs, and credit receipts: Watching a job.

The next chapter, How a Plan is declared, is a smaller one: the YAML recipe card that says which artifacts depend on which, for readers who will add or rearrange stations.

docs.title: How a Plan is declared
docs.text:
The last three chapters treated a Plan as a kitchen line: an ordered sequence of stations that consume and produce artifacts. This short chapter is the recipe card for that line — a YAML file that answers one question: in what order must artifacts exist?

You need this only if you are adding a Plan, rearranging stations, or debugging why a derived artifact did not run. Product decisions — whether a station is optional, whether its dish appears on the canvas — do not live here. They live next to the catalog, in code, because they are about what the product offers, not about dependency order.

docs.title: What the file is
docs.text:
Each YAML file in cloud_api/app/generation/plans/config/ declares one Plan. Every file uses the same schema; only the entries under artifacts differ.

At startup the Cloud API loads all of these files and registers each graph by the plan_id inside it. The file name is a convenience. Convention is {capability}.{engine}.yaml — for example data_analysis.pandas.yaml — but the authoritative id is the field in the file.

Think of the YAML as a bill of materials, not a program. It says “the computation graph depends on the Pandas code” the way a recipe says “the icing goes on after the cake.” It does not say “icing is optional if the guest declined dessert.” That second sentence is a request option, and request options are product behavior.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
plan_id: <capability>/<engine>
terminal_stage: <stage_id>        # always runs last; implemented in Python

artifacts:
  - kind: <artifact_kind>         # stable id this stage produces
    stage: <stage_id>             # station implementation id
    depends_on: [<artifact_kind>] # direct dependencies only (may be [])
Key Required Meaning plan_id yes Plan identifier; must match the Capability catalog terminal_stage yes Final station (persists results after per-call credit charges). Not listed under artifacts. artifacts yes Ordered list of station / artifact entries

Each artifacts entry:

Field Required Meaning kind yes Artifact kind produced by stage stage yes Registered station id on the Capability depends_on yes Artifact kinds that must exist before this station runs

Validation and other internal steps are ordinary entries in this list. The YAML does not mark them “internal.” Canvas visibility — whether the desktop shows the dish — is configured in plan_behavior.py, next to the catalog.

docs.title: An example: validating the graph
docs.text:
validate_dag checks the dag artifact and produces an internal analysis object the desktop never renders. In YAML that is only a dependency:

  - kind: analysis
    stage: validate_dag
    depends_on: [dag]

Whether this station runs at all depends on whether you asked for the graph. That gate is not in this file.

docs.title: How dependencies are interpreted
docs.text:
List only direct dependencies in depends_on. The loader checks that every referenced kind appears in the same file.

Independent branches (same depends_on) run in YAML list order once their dependencies are satisfied. If a dependency was requested but not produced — an optional station failed — dependent stations are skipped automatically rather than run on missing input.

docs.title: Adding a new Plan
docs.text:
1. Copy an existing YAML file and set a new plan_id.
  2. Fill artifacts with kind, stage, and depends_on only.
  3. Register station behavior (optional flags, request options, canvas artifacts) next to the catalog (plan_behavior.py).
  4. Register the Plan on the Capability.
  5. Implement any new stage ids on the Capability module.

Adjusting dependencies for an existing Plan is a YAML-only change. Changing which stations are optional, or which request option turns them on, is a Python-only change. Keeping those two questions in two places is deliberate: the recipe should not silently become the menu.

The conceptual chapters of the book end here. The next part is how a caller talks to the running system: Calling the Cloud API. If you are instead standing up the services, skip to Running the Cloud API yourself. If you still need to wire Google sign-in for the portal, that is Signing in.

docs.title: The parts of the system
docs.text:
The previous chapter explained why Nolain is split the way it is. This chapter is a map of what sits on each side of that split: the desktop, the local engine, the Cloud API, and the generation pipeline that turns an admitted question into artifacts.

If you have not read How Nolain is built, start there. The words Capability, Plan, Stage, artifact, sketch, and intent are used here with the meanings that chapter introduced.

This chapter does three things, in order. First it walks the path of a question through the running processes. Then it unpacks the generation framework — the menu, the kitchen line, the stations, the dishes. Finally it lists the pieces you will meet in the repository, and where later chapters go deeper.

docs.title: Two machines, one question
docs.text:
When you ask “What is total revenue by country?” two processes on your computer talk to a third process in the cloud.

The desktop app is what you see: file picker, question bar, results table, chart canvas. It does not compute the answer itself. It asks a local helper to describe the file, asks the Cloud API to produce a recipe, then asks the helper to run that recipe.

The local engine is that helper (a small Python service on port 8001). It is the only process that opens the file. It derives the sketch (column names, types, summaries, samples) and later executes the artifacts the cloud returned.

The Cloud API is the remote reasoning service (port 8000 in development). It never receives the file. It receives the question plus the sketch, decides whether to generate anything, and — if so — returns artifacts.

Around the Cloud API sit three supporting services:

  • Redis — short-lived memory for conversation sessions and generation jobs.
  • A background worker (Celery) — runs the Plan’s stages so the HTTP server does not block on model calls.
  • Supabase — who you are, whether your key is valid, how many credits remain.
  • OpenRouter — the single gateway for every language-model call. The product does not speak to OpenAI, DeepSeek, or anyone else directly.

A health endpoint (GET /health) reports whether Redis, the worker, and Supabase are reachable. Generation refuses to start (503) if Redis or the worker is down.

docs.title: The path of one question
docs.text:
Here is the same revenue question as a sequence, not a diagram. Each step is something a running system actually does.

  1. You load a file. The desktop asks the local engine for a sketch.
  2. You send a question. The desktop opens (or reuses) a conversation session on the Cloud API and posts the message, the sketch, and your toggles (computation graph on/off, chart on/off).
  3. Settlement checks the key. A portal-linked account with remaining credits is admitted. An empty balance is refused. A dedicated developer key may skip charging; see Credits and Billing internals.
  4. Dialogue classifies the turn. A single model call decides what kind of turn this is: refuse, answer from the sketch, explain a prior result, ask a clarifying question, or admit generation. Most turns stop here.
  5. If generation is admitted, policy builds a Plan. The model may have suggested a Capability and a Plan. The server checks the registry, applies your toggles, and rebuilds the pipeline. The model does not choose the stations.
  6. The worker runs the Plan. First station: write Pandas code, patch known compatibility issues, inspect the program without executing it. Optional stations: compile a computation graph from that code, write a chart contract, validate both. Last station: persist the artifacts and finish.
  7. The desktop polls until the job succeeds or fails, then executes locally against the file.
  8. The desktop reports the outcome back to the conversation. If execution failed and repair budget remains, the cloud queues a repair job without classifying the question again. The desktop polls and re-executes.
  9. Optionally, the desktop asks the cloud to wrap the numbers in a short narrative. If that call fails, you still have the table.

A conversation from start to finish repeats this loop with the actual HTTP calls. Direct generation endpoints (POST /api/v2/generate_dag) cover steps 5–7 without a session, without classification, and without the repair loop in step 8.

docs.title: The generation framework
docs.text: The control plane does not have an open-ended “do data science” prompt. It has a menu, a kitchen line, stations, and dishes. Those four ideas are Capability, Plan, Stage, and Artifact.

docs.title: Menu, line, station, dish
docs.text:
A restaurant is a useful picture:

In the restaurant In Nolain Today An item on the menu Capability — a product the cloud knows how to generate data_analysis: descriptive analysis of one CSV or Parquet file A kitchen line that prepares that item Plan — an engine: an ordered pipeline of stages data_analysis/pandas (implemented). data_analysis/ibis is on the menu but not staffed A station on that line Stage — a unit that consumes and produces artifacts Write the code; optionally compile a graph; optionally write a chart contract; validate; finish A dish that leaves a station Artifact — a typed output the desktop can use Executable Pandas code, optional computation graph, optional chart contract

A few consequences of this picture, which the rest of the system depends on:

  • Intent is not on the menu. Intent is the maître d’ deciding whether you sit down, get a glass of water from memory, or get sent to the kitchen. Mixing intent with Capability would let the maître d’ invent new dishes.
  • A chart is a side, not a second menu item. You toggle it on the same Plan. There is no “visualization Plan.”
  • Semantic analysis is a conversation with the waiter, before the ticket reaches the kitchen. It is not a Capability.
  • The chef does not redesign the line. Policy rebuilds the Plan from the registry and from your toggles (the admission step in app/generation/policy.py).

Optional artifacts on the Pandas Plan:

Your toggle What you get Compile DAG (default on) A computation-graph artifact (dag) Dashboard / chart (default on) A chart contract (visualization_spec)

The live menu is GET /api/v1/capabilities. Capabilities register themselves when the generation package loads.

docs.title: What the Pandas line produces
docs.text:
The primary dish is always executable analysis (code_pandas, returned to clients as pandas_code). Everything else is optional and derived.

Station Consumes Produces Calls a model? Optional? Write Pandas code — code_pandas Yes No. Static sandbox check; no execution on the server Compile DAG code_pandas dag Yes Yes, if you asked for the graph Format visualization code_pandas visualization_spec Yes Yes, if you asked for a chart Validate visualization visualization_spec internal check No With the chart Validate DAG dag internal check No With the graph Finalize code_pandas — No No. Persists produced artifacts after per-call charges

Dependencies between stations — “the graph cannot be compiled before the code exists” — are declared in a YAML recipe card. That card is the subject of How a Plan is declared. Whether a station is optional, and whether its dish appears on the canvas, is a product decision and lives next to the catalog, not in the recipe.

When code is regenerated (sandbox retry or runtime repair), derived dishes are thrown away and cooked again if you still asked for them. An old graph attached to new code would lie about what ran.

docs.title: How many model calls a job tends to make
docs.text:
These counts are the worker stations only. Classification and semantic reading, if they ran, are extra conversation-side calls.

Options Typical worker model calls Pandas only 1 (+ repairs if local execution fails) Pandas + graph 2 (code + compile); extra retries are separate budgets Pandas + chart, no graph 2 Pandas + graph + chart 3 or more

docs.title: Retry budgets
docs.text:
Retries are not one pool. Each failure mode has a different fix, so each has its own budget (configured in cloud_api/app/config/generation.yaml):

Budget Spent when Default Sandbox retries The worker rejects truncated, empty, or statically illegal code before it ships 2 Runtime-repair jobs The code shipped, the desktop ran it, and the real file threw an error 2 Compile / chart retries Graph or chart compilation or validation failed 2 Chain-wide ceiling Any Pandas generate-or-repair call, across the whole chain 9

A repair selects a profile by the kind of failure (syntax, Unicode, sandbox policy, runtime, truncation, …) and how many times it has already been tried. Surgical categories emit with reasoning disabled so hidden tokens cannot empty the completion. Runtime-repair jobs get a fresh sandbox budget so a depleted in-cloud budget cannot block a new attempt; they inherit the chain-wide attempt count so nested jobs cannot multiply forever.

docs.title: Dialogue: the maître d’
docs.text:
Every conversation turn starts with a classification: what kind of turn is this? That is one model call, on purpose. Most turns are off-topic, about the file’s structure, or requests for an explanation, and they should never reach the worker.

The classifier suggests; the server decides. For turns that look like generation, the model may propose a Capability and a Plan from the live catalog. Policy validates against the registry, applies your artifact toggles, and builds the Plan. The classifier is forbidden from turning on the graph or the chart: those are desktop toggles.

If classification fails to parse, the gate fails open (treat as a data question) so a real question is not dropped. A separate wording-based safety net can still refuse forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, or anomaly detection even if classification wanted to generate.

The branches:

Kind of turn Meaning Admits generation? Data question Clear, answerable question about the loaded file Yes, after semantic reading Execution feedback Prior result looks wrong Yes (regenerates with the feedback) Explanation Explain a prior result or how it was calculated No — uses stored outcome Meta question Structure answerable from the sketch alone (column list, row count, types) — not missing-value or quality checks No Out of scope Data-related, but no enabled Capability can serve it No Off-topic Unrelated to data analysis No Inappropriate Harmful content, prompt injection No Underspecified Data-related but too vague (“analyze my data”) No

A few boundary notes that surprise people:

  • “How many missing values in Customer ID?” is a data question, not a meta question. Null counts in the sketch are not the same as computing quality metrics.
  • Continuations that still request computation are data questions, not a separate “follow-up” product.
  • Only the two generation kinds carry a Capability and a Plan. Every other kind replies in text and never queues a worker job.

The conversation graph that implements this gate lives in the conversation manager (app/services/conversation_manager.py). Routing after classification is a small pure function (app/services/conversation_routing.py). The next chapter walks the HTTP loop the desktop uses; this chapter only needs you to know that a message is not a generation request until dialogue says so.

docs.title: Authentication and credits, in one paragraph
docs.text: Every workflow endpoint requires an API key (X-API-Key). Conversation routes check that credits remain without charging; each model call is charged the moment it completes. Portal-linked keys with an empty balance return HTTP 402. Unlinked non-developer keys return 402. Unlinked owner developer keys skip credit checks. Details: Billing internals. Portal account routes (/api/auth/*) use a Supabase sign-in token instead of the API key; see Signing in.

docs.title: Job memory
docs.text:
A generation job lives in Redis for one hour (job_state:{job_id}). A conversation session lives for 24 hours (conversation:{session_id}). The desktop polls GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} for progress. Useful statuses include queued, generating_code, compiling_from_code, formatting_visualization, validating, finalizing, success, failed, and cancelled. Cancellation is cooperative between stages; model calls already completed stay charged.

How to read a job — retries, token totals, credit receipts, worker logs — is Watching a job.

docs.title: Two APIs for the same Capability
docs.text:
Door What it is for Conversation (/api/v1/conversation/*) The desktop product: session, classification, clarification, local repair Direct generation (POST /api/v2/generate_dag) The same Capability without a chat: admit, synthesize, return artifacts Legacy (POST /api/v1/generate_dag) An older planner → compiler chain that does not use the Capability registry

Other useful endpoints: the model catalog (GET /api/v1/llm/models), the Capability catalog (GET /api/v1/capabilities), and standalone semantic analysis (POST /api/v1/analyze_query). Full request shapes and curl examples: Calling the Cloud API.

docs.title: Adding a second product
docs.text:
A second Capability (for example retrieval-augmented generation) would:

  1. Implement the Capability protocol and register it.
  2. Declare its Plans and optional artifacts.
  3. Enable it in policy.
  4. Reuse shared artifact types where they still fit.

Until that happens, out_of_scope is doing real work: the classifier sees the live catalog, and anything the catalog cannot serve returns a text message and does not admit generation. The Ibis Plan is the next engine for the same product, not a second product. It is catalogued and rejected until implemented.
