docs.text:
This table is a lookup, not a starting point. Ideas in this chapter come first; these are the files that implement them.

Concern Where it lives Typed artifacts cloud_api/app/generation/artifacts/ Plan catalog cloud_api/app/generation/plans/data_analysis.py Plan dependency graph (YAML) cloud_api/app/generation/plans/config/data_analysis.pandas.yaml Optional stages and canvas visibility cloud_api/app/generation/plans/plan_behavior.py Admission policy cloud_api/app/generation/policy.py Model catalog / OpenRouter cloud_api/app/config/llm_models.yaml, cloud_api/app/core/llm_config.py Pandas Capability cloud_api/app/generation/capabilities/data_analysis.py Static sandbox (inspect, do not execute) packages/query_execution/query_execution/pandas_code_policy.py Chart contract validation cloud_api/app/services/visualization_validator.py Retry budgets and repair profiles cloud_api/app/config/generation.yaml Conversation graph cloud_api/app/services/conversation_manager.py Intent types cloud_api/app/core/schema.py Classifier cloud_api/app/services/intent_classifier.py Out-of-scope safety net cloud_api/app/services/analysis_capabilities.py Worker tasks cloud_api/app/tasks/pandas_generation.py

The next chapter puts this map in motion: A conversation from start to finish. After that, How a Plan is declared is the recipe-card format for anyone adding or rearranging stations.

docs.title: How Nolain is built
docs.text:
This chapter is the design of the product, told as a story. It answers three questions in order: what the system is, why it is split the way it is, and how a question travels through it. The next chapter names the rooms in the house. This one explains why the house has those rooms.

You do not need to know the codebase. By the end you will have a small vocabulary — sketch, artifact, Capability, Plan, intent — and a picture of four layers that everything else hangs on.

docs.title: The core bet
docs.text:
Imagine a spreadsheet of invoices on your laptop. You want to ask “What is total revenue by country?” You do not want to upload the file to someone else’s warehouse. You also do not want a chatbot that invents a number.

Nolain’s bet is: local computation, remote reasoning.

Your machine keeps the file, derives a compact description of it, runs whatever analysis comes back, and shows the result. A remote service never sees the rows. It sees a sketch — column names, types, summaries, a handful of sample values — plus your question. It returns artifacts: executable analysis, and if you asked for them, a computation graph and a chart contract. Your machine runs those artifacts against the real file.

The analogy is a librarian and a reading room. You do not ship the books to a consultant. You send the card catalog. The consultant writes a procedure (“pull these shelves, add these columns, rank the result”). You run the procedure in the room that actually has the books. The answer is true because it was computed there, not because the consultant asserted it.

That split is the product. Everything below is how the split is kept reliable, cheap enough, and hard to misuse.

docs.title: Four layers
docs.text:
Think of four floors, from closest to you (and to the file) to farthest from the data.

Local layer          owns the file, derives the sketch, runs artifacts, shows results
Dialogue layer       decides whether this turn should generate anything
Synthesis layer      once admitted, produces typed artifacts
Settlement layer     who is calling, which model, what the reasoning costs

The data plane is the local layer: own the file, compute, report. The control plane is dialogue + synthesis + settlement: reason, admit, charge. The sketch is the only interface between them. If a change requires the control plane to see more of the file, it is fighting this design.

docs.title: Local layer
docs.text:
What it does. Own the file. Derive the sketch. Execute artifacts. Show results. Report what happened.

This is the only place that may touch the full dataset. It is also the only place whose output counts as an answer: a number, a table, a chart from real rows.

What it refuses. It does not invent analysis. It does not call models. It does not decide product scope. If synthesis returns nothing executable, this layer has nothing to run.

Why it is strong. Privacy is structural, not a policy checkbox. Execution latency is local. The engine can grow without teaching the remote side about your rows.

The tradeoff. Generation quality is capped by the sketch. Rare values and file-specific quirks that never appear in samples will surprise the model. Sending the file would raise hit rate and destroy the privacy bet.

docs.title: Dialogue layer
docs.text:
What it does. Treat each user turn as a conversation decision, not as a generation request. Classify what kind of turn this is. Answer from the sketch when that is enough. Refuse what is off-topic, harmful, underspecified, or outside enabled products. Ask for clarification when the question is ambiguous. Only then admit generation.

This layer is a gate. Most turns should never reach synthesis. That is a cost decision and a safety decision.

What it refuses. It does not pick pipelines or optional artifacts. “The user wants a chart” is not “invent a visualization product.” Optional outputs are your choices (and the desktop’s toggles), not the model’s.

Why it is strong. The conversation can be useful without a generation job: column lists, explanations of a prior result, a clear “we don’t do that yet.” New products can appear in the catalog without turning the gate into a planner.

The tradeoff. If classification breaks, the gate fails open: it treats the turn as a data question so a real question is not silently dropped. That spends money and can admit work that should have been refused. Clarification adds a turn — and a charge — before any artifact exists.

docs.title: Synthesis layer
docs.text:
What it does. Once generation is admitted, produce typed artifacts under a registered Capability, through a Plan. Policy rebuilds the Plan. The model fills in artifacts; it does not design the machine that produces them.

Three words, used the same way for the rest of the book:

  • A Capability is a product on the menu. Today: “descriptive analysis of one file.”
  • A Plan is a kitchen line for that product. Today: the Pandas line. Another line (Ibis) is catalogued and refused until it is implemented.
  • A Stage is a station on that line. Stations consume and produce artifacts. Optional artifacts (graph, chart) are request options on a Plan, not extra menu items.

What it refuses. The model does not select Capabilities, Plans, or the shape of the pipeline. Unknown or unimplemented Plans are rejected. A dashboard is an artifact, not a Plan. Understanding the question (semantic analysis) happens before admission; it is not itself a Capability.

Why it is strong. One Plan can grow optional outputs without a combinatorial explosion of products. Deterministic checks sit next to generative steps so retries have something other than “try again” to push against.

The tradeoff. Code-first means the graph can drift from what actually ran, and a chart contract can disagree with both. Repair re-generates from the failure, not from a deeper reading of the question.

docs.title: Settlement layer
docs.text:
What it does. Know who is calling. Offer a catalog of models. Charge for reasoning work as it happens (each model call), not for “a query” as a lump. Keep the control plane from doing work it cannot bill or should not admit.

What it refuses. This layer does not execute data. It does not decide whether a question is in scope. A caller with no portal account (except a dedicated developer credential) does not get a path through. An empty credit balance does not get another job.

Why it is strong. One model gateway keeps the product from growing a provider-shaped codebase. Charging per call matches actual cost: a job with a graph and a chart is several calls, not one.

The tradeoff. Price follows token usage, so the same question costs different amounts on different models and on retry-heavy paths. Conversation memory that lives in a short-lived store will vanish.

docs.title: How a question travels
docs.text:
The system is a loop between the data plane and the control plane. The file never crosses that boundary. Artifacts and a sketch do.

The walkthrough below uses one example: you have loaded a retail invoice file, and you ask “What are the top 5 countries by total revenue?”

docs.title: 1. Presence — the file becomes a sketch
docs.text:
You load the table on the desktop. The local layer reads it and produces a sketch: column names (Country, Quantity, Price, …), types, summaries, sample values. That sketch is what every later layer is allowed to see.

If the sketch is wrong or thin, every downstream step inherits that error. The full file does not leave the machine.

docs.title: 2. Identity — settlement before work
docs.text:
Before any conversation turn or generation, settlement asks: is this a known caller, and may they spend?

Caller Admitted? Charged for model work? Portal-linked account with remaining credits Yes Yes Portal-linked account with empty balance No — Unlinked non-developer credential No — Dedicated unlinked developer credential Yes No

Queueing work is not itself a charge. Every model call that does run is charged as soon as it completes, including calls that later look wasted (a compile that fails, a gate that then refuses). Local execution is never a cloud charge.

docs.title: 3. Session — dialogue binds a sketch to a thread
docs.text:
Dialogue opens a session: a short-lived memory of messages, the current sketch, and (later) the last result. No model call is required to open it.

The session is not a durable account object. It expires (24 hours on the server). Follow-ups and explanations are only as good as what that memory still holds.

docs.title: 4. A turn — dialogue decides the branch
docs.text:
You send the question. The desktop also sends the current sketch and your choices about optional artifacts (whether you want a computation graph, whether you want a chart). Those choices belong to you, not to the model.

Dialogue classifies the turn once, then branches. Classification is a model call (settlement charges it). A wording-based safety override can still force “out of product” even if classification wanted to generate.

For our revenue question, the turn is a clear data question. Other turns take other doors:

Kind of turn What happens Reaches synthesis? Off-topic, harmful, or too vague A short refusal, or a prompt for a better question No Answerable from the sketch alone (columns, row count, types) Answer from metadata; no generation No Explain a prior result or method Grounded text from stored outcome No Data-related, but no enabled Capability can serve it Named refusal (forecasting, inference, optimization, anomaly detection, …) No Ambiguous data question Ask for clarification; wait for the next turn Not yet Clear data question Semantic reading of the question, then admission Yes, if still clear “That result looks wrong” Treat as a new generation with the prior question plus the feedback Yes

A user message is not a generation request until this layer says so. The classifier may suggest a Capability and a Plan. It must not choose optional artifacts, and it must not invent a product. Policy, not the prompt, is authoritative.

Fail-open. If classification fails to parse, dialogue treats the turn as a data question and continues toward admission. That spends money in order not to drop a real question.

Clarification shortcut. Once you have answered a clarification, the next send may skip classification and semantic reading and go straight to admission. The question’s meaning is treated as settled.

docs.title: 5. Admission — policy, not the model, builds the Plan
docs.text:
For generation turns, a second look at the question (semantic analysis) may still stop the flow: if terms are ambiguous (“revenue” could mean several things), dialogue asks; if that reading fails, it answers in text and does not generate.

If the question is clear, policy admits:

  1. The Capability must be registered and enabled. Unknown ids fall back to the one enabled product (descriptive analysis of one file).
  2. The Plan must be a known engine for that product. An unimplemented engine is rejected, not approximated.
  3. Optional artifacts come from the client’s toggles, not from the classifier.
  4. The server rebuilds the Plan. The model never selects the pipeline.

There is one enabled Capability today. Everything else is out of scope until a new Capability is registered and enabled. A chart is not a different product; it is an optional artifact on the same Plan.

docs.title: 6. Synthesis — artifacts, checks, bounded retries
docs.text:
Admitted work produces artifacts under the Plan:

  1. Primary artifact: executable analysis (Pandas code) from the question and the sketch.
  2. Optional graph: a computation-graph view derived from that code, if you asked for it.
  3. Optional chart contract: a renderer-neutral spec, if you asked for it.

After each generative step, a deterministic check may reject the artifact (a static sandbox on code, which inspects the program without running your data; structural validation of the graph; contract validation of the chart). Rejection spends a retry budget and re-runs the generative step that produced the bad artifact.

Two budgets exist and do not borrow from each other:

  • a budget for producing executable analysis (also shared with local-exec repair, below);
  • a budget for graph/chart compilation and validation.

Synthesis does not execute your file. It may only inspect the sketch and the artifacts it has already produced. Code that fails the static sandbox never ships. When analysis is regenerated, derived artifacts (graph, chart) are invalidated and must be produced again if still requested.

Each model call inside this work is charged immediately. A failed compile still costs. Local execution, when it happens, does not.

docs.title: 7. Execution — only the local layer may compute
docs.text:
The desktop receives artifacts and runs them against the real file. That is the first moment the analysis meets the data.

A successful job on the control plane is not an answer. The local result is. The control plane is not charged for this step.

docs.title: 8. Report and repair — execution feedback without reopening the gate
docs.text:
After every local run, success or failure, the desktop tells dialogue what happened. A successful result is stored for later explanation and follow-up.

If execution failed, and the analysis-retry budget still has remaining attempts, dialogue does not classify again. It sends the failed artifact and the error back to synthesis (a repair). The desktop waits, executes the new artifacts, and reports again, until the run succeeds or the budget is exhausted.

Kind of correction When Re-enters dialogue classification? Internal synthesis retry Artifact rejected by a static check before it ships No Runtime repair Artifact passed checks but failed on the real file No

Repair cannot change what the question meant. It cannot spend more than the remaining budget. It cannot turn a data question into a different Capability.

docs.title: 9. Framing — narrative is optional and after the fact
docs.text: Once a result exists, the desktop may ask for a narrative wrapping. That is another model call (charged). It must not replace the executed result. If framing fails, you still have the numbers.

docs.title: Two doors into the same product
docs.text:
The loop above is the conversation path — what the desktop app uses.

There is also a direct generation path: skip session and dialogue, admit a Capability from the request, run synthesis, return artifacts. That path does not classify, does not clarify, and does not run the local repair loop. It is the same product with the gate and the memory stripped off.

Those two paths must not silently become two products. Direct generation is the same Capability and the same artifacts; it is honest about omitting the gate.

docs.title: Steering policies
docs.text:
The philosophy is not only layers and workflow. It is also explicit decisions that aim the system: what to optimize on the happy path, what to spend when something fails, and what must never be delegated to the model.

These decisions live in configuration and in code. The important part is the direction, not the knob name. Changing a steering policy is a product bet — “we now value X over Y” — not a cosmetic tweak.

docs.title: Emit fast, keep repairs executable
docs.text:
Decision. First-pass artifact generation uses minimal model reasoning. Surgical repairs — syntax, invalid unicode, sandbox policy, and runtime column/name fixes — also emit with reasoning disabled. Hidden reasoning is not spent on those paths because reasoning tokens share the completion budget and can starve the visible program.

Why. First pass is emission: turn a clear question and a sketch into executable analysis. Extra “thinking” mostly adds latency and cost without improving code that must pass deterministic checks anyway. A typo, a zero-width space, or a bad column name is still emission of a short corrected program, not open-ended diagnosis.

Direction. Prefer cheap, direct generation. Pay for longer visible completions on repair rather than hidden reasoning. Deterministic fixes (strip illegal format characters, localize runtime line numbers) run before any model retry.

docs.title: Separate retry budgets
docs.text:
Decision. Retries are not one pool. Analysis has distinct budgets for (a) in-cloud rejection before anything ships, (b) local execution failure reported back, and (c) graph/chart compile and validation. Pandas calls also share a chain-wide ceiling so nested repair jobs cannot multiply total model calls.

Why. A compile loop should not consume the user’s allowance for “the code was right but my file surprised you.” A sandbox reject should not exhaust the budget for real execution feedback. Each failure mode has a different fix.

Direction. Failures are bounded and typed. Source budgets preserve the meaning of each retry; the chain ceiling bounds total cost.

docs.title: Checks before ship, execution only local
docs.text:
Decision. Executable analysis is inspected on the control plane with static policy (no running the user’s data in the cloud). Graph and chart contracts get deterministic validation after generative steps. Only the local layer runs against the file.

Why. The privacy bet forbids cloud execution on full data. Static rejection catches a large class of unsafe or unusable code early. Validation gives retries a concrete error, not “try again.” Local execution is the ground truth the sketch could not provide.

Direction. Trust is staged: sketch → generated artifact → checked artifact → executed result. Each stage can send work backward; none skips straight to “believe the model.”

docs.title: Regenerate downstream when upstream changes
docs.text:
Decision. When executable analysis is regenerated (repair or sandbox retry), derived artifacts — graph, chart — are invalidated and rebuilt if still requested.

Why. Derived views are projections of the analysis. Keeping an old graph attached to new code would lie about what ran.

Direction. One primary artifact anchors truth; everything else follows it or disappears.

docs.title: Model catalog vs repair profile
docs.text:
Decision. The model catalog sets defaults for which models exist, default reasoning per model, and routing preferences. Pandas repair selects a profile from the kind of failure and how many times it has already been tried. Syntax, Unicode, sandbox-policy, and first runtime repairs emit compact code with reasoning disabled.

Why. Catalog defaults optimize the common case across all call sites (classifier, semantic reading, compile, chart format). Repair is a different job with different economics.

Direction. Defaults are for throughput; evidence from the actual failure chooses the recovery budget.

docs.title: Charge the call, not the question
docs.text:
Decision. Every model invocation settles immediately when it completes. Queueing synthesis is not a charge. Local execution is never a charge. A margin (surplus) is applied on top of raw token cost.

Why. Vendor cost is per call. Hiding failed compiles or gate calls inside a flat “query price” would misalign product and infrastructure.

Direction. Users pay for reasoning work that actually happened.

docs.title: Gate: fail-open, then narrow
docs.text:
Decision. If intent classification breaks, treat the turn as a data question and continue toward admission. A separate wording-based safety layer can still refuse forecasting, inference, optimization, and anomaly detection. Optional artifacts stay with the user; classification does not turn them on.

Why. Fail-open favors not losing real questions over not spending on junk. The safety layer catches a small set of high-risk asks that should never reach synthesis even when classification misfires. Optional artifacts stay with the user so the gate cannot silently turn on expensive outputs.

Direction. The conversation gate is permissive on machinery failure, strict on product boundary, silent on user toggles.

docs.title: Admission is server-side
docs.text:
Decision. Models may suggest a Capability and Plan; policy rebuilds the Plan from the registry and client toggles. Only enabled Capabilities admit. Unknown Plans reject; unimplemented Plans reject.

Why. Prompts drift; registries do not. Letting the model pick pipelines would make every new product a prompt edit instead of a registration.

Direction. Extensibility through registration, not through chat creativity.

docs.title: Reasoning-capable models still emit on the happy path
docs.text:
Decision. Even when the chosen model supports extended reasoning, code and JSON emitters default to no extra reasoning effort on first pass and on surgical Pandas repairs. Heavier models in the catalog may use more reasoning for tasks that need it (for example explanation paths).

Why. Reasoning tokens are expensive and invisible until they fail. For structured output that will be validated anyway, thinking is often waste.

Direction. Use the model’s strength for output quality and validation loops, not for open-ended cogitation on every turn.

docs.title: Where steering lives, and what a change means
docs.text:
Tunable steering (retry budgets, chain attempt ceiling, repair profiles, model defaults, credit formula) lives in policy files loaded at startup. Structural rules (admission, failure classification, sandbox, intent routing, charge timing) live in code. The next chapter maps file to concern; this chapter maps decision to intent.

When you change a value, ask: which direction does this push?

If you increase… You are saying… Repair reasoning effort Failures deserve more diagnosis; accept higher cost on the error path Sandbox retry budget Reject early, retry often, before the user ever runs code Exec-repair budget Local truth matters; keep trying after the sketch misled generation Compile/chart retry budget Derived artifacts must be structurally valid, not just plausible Default reasoning on emitters Willing to pay latency/cost on every first pass for possibly better code Surplus rate Pricing should carry more buffer above vendor cost Fail-open → fail-closed Prefer refusing ambiguous turns over spending on possible junk

docs.title: Rules the workflow may not work around
docs.text:
Changing these is a philosophy change, not a tweak.

Data

  • The file stays local. The sketch is the only remote view of the data.
  • One loaded table is the unit of analysis.
  • Enabled product: descriptive work on that table (aggregations, comparisons, rankings, trends, quality checks, reshape, optional charts).
  • Not enabled until a Capability says so: forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, anomaly detection, and anything else the catalog does not name.

Authority

  • Models propose; policy admits. Registries and client options are the source of truth.
  • Intent (conversation branch) is not a Capability (generation product). Mixing them would let a prompt invent a pipeline.
  • Optional artifacts are user/desktop toggles on one Plan, not new Plans and not classifier output.
  • Unimplemented Plans are rejected. Unknown Capabilities fall back to the enabled default; they are not invented.

Generation

  • Generation is admitted, not assumed.
  • Semantic reading of the question is a gate, not a product.
  • Executable analysis is primary; graph and chart are derived and optional.
  • Static checks must pass before an artifact ships. Execution happens only locally.
  • Fail-open on classifier failure; wording-based safety may still refuse an admitted-looking data question.

Repair and memory

  • Runtime repair is execution feedback, not a new conversation.
  • Dialogue memory is short-lived and weakly bound to the caller.
  • Cooperative cancellation may stop work between steps; model calls already completed stay charged.

Settlement

  • Charge the reasoning, not the job. Each model call settles when it completes.
  • Empty balance: no further admitted work.
  • Local execution is free to the cloud.
  • Developer credentials that are not tied to a portal account skip settlement; every other caller does not.

docs.title: Strengths, assumptions, tradeoffs
docs.text:
Strengths. Structural privacy. Answers grounded in execution. A conversation that can refuse. A small, explicit product surface. Deterministic belts around generative steps. Cost aligned with work.

Assumptions. The sketch is representative enough, often enough. A single executable-analysis engine is a sufficient lingua franca between control plane and data plane. The desktop is a trusted partner: it executes, it reports, it owns optional-artifact toggles. Bounded retries and a fail-open gate are preferable to silent refusal. Users will accept paying for the gate and for failed steps because those were real model calls.

Choice What it buys What it costs Sketch only, never the file Privacy, simpler trust, local truth Missed quirks; generation can be locally wrong Intent gate before generation Cheap refusals; clearer product boundary Extra calls; fail-open can admit junk Classifier suggests, policy admits The model cannot invent pipelines Catalog and policy must stay the real source of truth Optional artifacts, not extra Plans One Plan, many outputs Options must be carried on every turn Analysis first, graph and chart derived Fast path to something executable Drift between code, graph, and spec Repair without re-classifying Fast correction on exec errors Repair cannot change the question’s meaning Charge every model call immediately Matches vendor cost Users pay for failed steps and for the gate itself Short-lived session memory Simple operations History is not a durable account object Single enabled Capability Honest “out of scope” Dialogue must keep saying no Direct generation beside conversation Same artifacts without a chat Two paths that can drift if they are not kept honest

docs.title: Room for improvement
docs.text:
The current shape is a working compromise, not a finished architecture.

The sketch is still a sketch. Better summaries, better samples, and honest signals about data quality would raise hit rate without moving the file.

One Capability is both a strength and a ceiling. “Out of scope” is doing a lot of work. A second product will test whether intent, policy, and artifacts actually compose.

A second engine is a promise. Until another Plan is implemented, “Plan = engine” is vocabulary, not a proven split.

Code, graph, and chart can disagree. Treating the graph as a projection is convenient. Making it the executable source of truth would make the canvas trustworthy. That is not done.

Dialogue is a good gate and a weak memory. Sessions expire, ownership is weakly bound, and follow-up quality depends on whatever was last stored.

Fail-open and wording-based safety are temporary ethics. Admission should eventually fail closed on classifier failure. Out-of-scope should come from the Capability catalog, not from phrase lists.

Settlement is call-shaped; the product is still question-shaped. Clearer receipts and budgets per question would make “pay for reasoning” feel like a product.

The local layer is trusted more than it is isolated. Policy can constrain what ships; it cannot make local execution a full sandbox of an untrusted world.

docs.title: If you are changing the product
docs.text:
When adding a feature or changing a configured value, ask:

  1. Which layer owns it?
  2. Which steering policy does it extend or contradict?

Layer ownership:

  • If it touches the file or the result, it belongs in the local layer.
  • If it decides whether to generate, it belongs in dialogue.
  • If it produces something executable or viewable, it belongs in synthesis — not a new intent, and not a new Plan for a toggle.
  • If it is about who pays or which model runs, it belongs in settlement.

If a change requires the control plane to see more of the file, the model to pick a pipeline, a new Plan for what is really an optional artifact, or a second entry path with different semantics, it is fighting this philosophy. That can still be the right call — but it should be named as a bet change, not as a small addition.

The next chapter, The parts of the system, takes this design and names the components: desktop, local engine, Cloud API, generation pipeline, and how a Capability is admitted. After that, A conversation from start to finish walks one question through every HTTP step the desktop actually takes.

docs.title: Calling the Cloud API
docs.text:
The previous chapters explained what Nolain is and how a question travels through it. This chapter is the HTTP reference: how a caller authenticates, which doors exist, and what a request looks like.

There are two doors into the same product.

  • Conversation is what the desktop uses. You open a session on a sketch, send a message, and the server decides whether to reply in text, ask a clarifying question, or queue a generation job. After local execution you report the outcome; the server may repair. This is the full loop in A conversation from start to finish.
  • Direct generation skips the session and the gate. You admit a Capability, poll for artifacts, and execute them yourself. Same dishes, no maître d’, no repair loop.

Both doors receive a sketch (metadata), never the file. Both return artifacts: Pandas code, and optionally a computation graph and a chart contract. Interactive OpenAPI lives at http://localhost:8000/docs.

Related chapters: Credits (what a call costs), Billing internals (how charging is implemented), Watching a job (how to read status), Signing in (portal tokens).

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Every request to /api/v1/* or /api/v2/* carries an API key:

-H "X-API-Key: <your-api-key>"

Keys come from the Nolain portal, or from POST /api/auth/keys once you are signed in. Portal account routes under /api/auth/* use a Supabase access token instead:

-H "Authorization: Bearer <access_token>"

The exception is GET /api/auth/key-status, which authenticates with X-API-Key (the desktop Settings panel).

docs.title: Who may spend credits
docs.text:
Consumption is account-based for portal-linked keys. Admission reads the profile balance and returns 402 Payment Required when it is empty.

Key type Admitted? Charged per model call? Portal-linked (user_id set) Requires remaining credits Yes Unlinked owner (tier = owner, no user_id) Always No Unlinked non-owner 402 —

Monthly plan grants: Free 1,000 credits, Premium 50,000. See Credits.

Queueing a job does not consume credits by itself. Each model call is charged from token usage plus surplus as soon as it completes.

All model traffic routes through OpenRouter. Pass an optional model field (a catalog id from GET /api/v1/llm/models); omit it to use the server default.

docs.title: Health and catalogs
docs.text: These endpoints do not generate analysis. They tell you whether the system is up, which models you may pick, and which products the server currently admits.

docs.title: GET / — service status
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:8000/

{
  "app": "Data Query DAG Generator API",
  "status": "online",
  "documentation": "/docs"
}

docs.title: GET /health — runtime health
docs.text:
Reports Redis, Celery workers, and Supabase. Generation endpoints return 503 when Redis or a worker is unavailable.

curl http://localhost:8000/health

{
  "status": "ok",
  "services": {
    "redis": { "ok": true },
    "celery": { "ok": true, "workers": ["celery@host"] },
    "supabase": { "ok": true, "host": "your-project.supabase.co" }
  }
}

status is "degraded" when any listed service is not ok.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/llm/models — model catalog
docs.text:
Lists selectable models and the server default. Authentication only; does not require remaining credits.

curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/llm/models \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here"

{
  "provider": "openrouter",
  "default_model_id": "deepseek-v4-flash-0731",
  "models": [
    { "id": "deepseek-v4-flash-0731", "label": "DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731)", "openrouter_model": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731", "default": true },
    { "id": "gpt-5.6-luna", "label": "GPT-5.6 Luna", "openrouter_model": "openai/gpt-5.6-luna" }
  ]
}

docs.title: GET /api/v1/capabilities — Capability / Plan catalog
docs.text:
Lists registered generation products, their engines, and optional artifacts. Optional artifacts (graph, chart contract) are request options on a Plan, not extra Plan ids.

curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/capabilities \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here"

{
  "capabilities": [
    {
      "id": "data_analysis",
      "enabled": true,
      "plans": [
        {
          "plan_id": "data_analysis/pandas",
          "selectable": true,
          "default": true,
          "implemented": true,
          "engine": "pandas",
          "stages": ["generate_pandas", "compile_dag", "format_visualization", "validate_visualization", "validate_dag", "finalize_plan"],
          "optional_stages": ["compile_dag", "format_visualization", "validate_visualization"],
          "optional_artifacts": ["dag", "visualization_spec"],
          "terminal_artifact_kinds": ["code_pandas", "dag", "visualization_spec"]
        },
        {
          "plan_id": "data_analysis/ibis",
          "selectable": false,
          "implemented": false
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

data_analysis/ibis is catalogued but not selectable. Older Plan ids such as data_analysis/analysis/with_dag map onto data_analysis/pandas plus options.

docs.title: Conversation: the desktop loop
docs.text: This is the path A conversation from start to finish described. Sessions live in Redis for 24 hours. Session GET/DELETE currently do not verify that the calling key created the session.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/conversation/start
docs.text:
Creates a session. No model call; no charge.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/conversation/start \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here" \
  -d '{ "metadata": { "available_columns": ["Country", "Price"] } }'

{ "session_id": "c0a1b2c3-d4e5-6789-abcd-ef1234567890" }

docs.title: POST /api/v1/conversation/message
docs.text:
The main decision: classify the turn (unless you are answering a clarification) and maybe admit a job.

Field Type Required Description session_id string yes From /start message string yes The user’s text metadata object yes The sketch (see Metadata) model string no Catalog model id clarifications array no When set, skips classify/semantic and queues generation compile_dag boolean no Compile-DAG toggle (default true) include_visualization boolean no Request a chart spec (default true) plan_id string no Optional catalog Plan (default data_analysis/pandas)

The graph and chart toggles are yours. The classifier may suggest a Capability and a Plan; it does not override these options.

Without clarifications, the server classifies intent and returns one of:

type in response Meaning text_response Off-topic, unsafe, underspecified, explanation, out of scope, or semantic failure meta_answer Structure question answered from the sketch clarification Ambiguous terms; resend with clarifications generation Job accepted; poll task_id 
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/conversation/message \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here" \
  -d '{
    "session_id": "c0a1b2c3-d4e5-6789-abcd-ef1234567890",
    "message": "Show a bar chart of the top 5 countries by total revenue",
    "metadata": { "available_columns": ["Country", "Quantity", "Price"] },
    "compile_dag": true
  }'

{
  "type": "generation",
  "task_id": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890",
  "session_id": "c0a1b2c3-d4e5-6789-abcd-ef1234567890",
  "capability_id": "data_analysis",
  "plan_id": "data_analysis/pandas",
  "compile_dag": true,
  "include_visualization": true
}

Requests no registered Capability can serve return text_response and do not queue generation. Forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection currently fall in that branch. Explanation requests return grounded text from saved result context and do not queue generation.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/conversation/result
docs.text:
Notify the server of local execution so follow-ups have context. No charge on a successful store.

When exec_error and pandas_code are set, the previous generation job succeeded, that job still has pandas_retries_left > 0, and the chain has not reached its attempt ceiling, the server queues a repair job (same question, failed code plus traceback, no classifier). Jobs that already failed in the cloud are not re-queued as runtime repairs. The response:

{
  "status": "repairing",
  "type": "generation",
  "task_id": "...",
  "session_id": "...",
  "capability_id": "data_analysis",
  "plan_id": "data_analysis/pandas",
  "compile_dag": true,
  "include_visualization": true,
  "pandas_retries_left": 1
}

Poll that task_id and re-execute locally. If no retries remain, the response is { "status": "ok" }.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/conversation/result \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here" \
  -d '{
    "session_id": "c0a1b2c3-d4e5-6789-abcd-ef1234567890",
    "dag": { "graph_id": "...", "nodes": [], "output_node": "node_2" },
    "exec_result": { "preview": [{"Country": "United Kingdom", "revenue": 912345.0}] },
    "pandas_code": "result = df.groupby('Country')['Quantity'].sum()"
  }'

docs.title: POST /api/v1/conversation/synthesize
docs.text:
Optional post-execution framing. Charges credits if a model is invoked. On failure the endpoint still returns { "status": "success", "narrative": {} }.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/conversation/synthesize \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here" \
  -d '{
    "session_id": "c0a1b2c3-d4e5-6789-abcd-ef1234567890",
    "question": "What are the top 5 countries by total revenue?",
    "result_summary": "United Kingdom leads, followed by France.",
    "outcome": "answered",
    "model": "deepseek-v4-flash-0731"
  }'

docs.title: GET / DELETE /api/v1/conversation/{session_id}
docs.text: Read or delete the Redis session. Delete returns { "status": "deleted" }. Missing session on GET returns 404.

docs.title: Direct generation
docs.text:
Use this door when you already know you want artifacts and do not need a chat. Prefer POST /api/v2/generate_dag. The v1 endpoint is a legacy planner → compiler chain that does not use the Capability registry.

Both are asynchronous: they return a task_id. Poll GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} (next section) for artifacts.

docs.title: POST /api/v2/generate_dag — registered Capability
docs.text:
Admits data_analysis. The server builds a Plan of stages from request options. The Pandas Plan always produces executable code. Optional stages add a graph and/or a chart contract. Each worker model call is charged as it completes; poll billing.charged_credits for the running total.

Stations, in order, when every optional is on:

  1. Write Pandas code from the question and the sketch. Compatibility patches and a static sandbox check (no execution on the server). Truncated, empty, illegal, or incomplete code is rejected and may retry.
  2. Compile a computation graph from that code (compile_dag=true, default).
  3. Write a chart contract (include_visualization=true, default).
  4. Validate the chart contract.
  5. Validate the graph.
  6. Persist artifacts and finish.

A chart is a toggle, not a different Plan.

docs.title: Billing internals
docs.text:
The user-facing unit, monthly allowances, and worked examples are in Credits. This chapter is for someone who needs to change that system: the formula, where rates come from, who is admitted, and how a receipt is written.

What billing is. Every time the product calls a language model, two things happen: OpenRouter runs the model (that costs the operator money), and the app subtracts credits from the user’s account so they pay for that call. A typical Pandas job with a chart and a graph is several calls, not one. Each call takes some credits.

Why it is built this way. Vendor cost is per call. Hiding failed compiles or gate calls inside a flat “query price” would misalign the product with the infrastructure. The ledger is the source of truth; Redis job totals are a running scoreboard.

The rest of the chapter is the formula, the rate sources, who may spend, how receipts are tagged, and how to test a change.

docs.title: Credit formula
docs.text:
The amount deducted for one model call is the token cost converted to credits, plus a surplus (the platform margin). Both parts round up.

token_credits = ceil(model_token_cost_usd × credits_per_dollar)
surplus_credits = ceil(token_credits × surplus_rate)     # default 1.0 (100%)
charged_credits = token_credits + surplus_credits      # 0 if token_credits is 0

Policy: app/config/billing.yaml (env overrides: CREDITS_PER_DOLLAR, CREDIT_SURPLUS_RATE, BILLING_CONFIG).

Setting Default Env override credits_per_dollar 1000 CREDITS_PER_DOLLAR surplus_rate 1.0 CREDIT_SURPLUS_RATE MONTHLY_PLAN_CREDITS["free"] 1000 — MONTHLY_PLAN_CREDITS["premium"] 50000 —

docs.title: Model token rates
docs.text:
Primary source: OpenRouter GET /api/v1/models (pricing keyed by each catalog model's openrouter_model slug in llm_models.yaml).

Fallback: billing.yaml → pricing.model_overrides (USD per 1M tokens).

Set pricing.source: yaml to use overrides only (tests, offline).

Implementation: app/core/openrouter_pricing.py, app/core/credit_pricing.py.

docs.title: Consumption
docs.text:
Billable API keys must be portal-linked (clients_nolain_query.user_id set). Admission reads profiles_nolain_query.credit_balance and returns HTTP 402 when the balance is empty.

Unlinked owner keys (developer keys from scripts/ensure-developer-key.sql, with tier = 'owner' and no user_id) skip credit admission and settlement. Linked owner keys follow the same rules as free/premium portal keys.

Unlinked non-owner keys are rejected with 402 (no portal account).

Charge timing: every LLM invoke inside an active billing_scope(client_id). Workers wrap stage execution; HTTP handlers wrap conversation, analyze_query, and synthesize.

Credit charges use the atomic RPCs in sql/003_account_balance.sql. Existing databases that still have query_balance should apply sql/008_credit_rename.sql. Configure Stripe packages as a JSON map, for example {"price_basic":"1000","price_team":"10000"}. The webhook accepts only paid sessions whose price_id and declared credits match this map.

docs.title: Receipts: one job, many LLM charges
docs.text:
Every time the product calls an LLM (code generation, DAG, chart, and so on), two things happen:

  1. OpenRouter runs the model. That costs us money.
  2. The app then subtracts credits from the user's account so they pay for that call.

A typical pandas job with a chart and a DAG is several LLM calls, not one. Each call should take some credits.

Two stores are involved:

  • User balance (credit_balance) — a number: how many credits the user has left.
  • Ledger (credit_balance_ledger_nolain_query) — the receipt book. Each charge adds a row: “minus 6 credits for job X”, then “minus 4 credits for the same job”, and so on.

When a charge works, both update: the balance goes down, and a new receipt is added. The receipt stores the job id so you can later ask what that query cost by summing its rows.

Receipts are tagged with event_type:

Tag Meaning llm_call One LLM call was charged. A job may have many of these. grant Credits were added (plan or Stripe top-up). settlement Reserved. At most one row of this tag per job.

The database still has a rule: at most one settlement receipt per job. That is unused today. It is kept for a future “one total row for the whole job” if we ever need it. Per-call charges use llm_call, which that rule does not cover, so a job can have many receipts.

If a later LLM call in the same job were written as settlement, the database would reject it (HTTP 409). The job would skip that stage even though the model already ran. Conversation endpoints that omit job_id never hit this rule.

Redis job billing totals are only a running scoreboard. They do not decide whether a second charge is allowed. The ledger does.

docs.title: Manual testing
docs.text:
1. Grant credits: update profiles_nolain_query set credit_balance = 1000 ...
  2. Run a pandas-only job (compile_dag: false, include_visualization: false).
  3. Poll GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{job_id} until success.
  4. Expect billing.charged_credits reflecting all LLM calls in the job.
  5. Repeat with compile_dag: true — expect higher totals (more LLM calls + tokens).
cd cloud_api && PYTHONPATH=. pytest -q

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: Admission requires a positive credit balance for portal-linked keys. Unlinked owner developer keys skip admission and settlement. Each LLM credit charge is atomic; if writing the receipt fails, the call fails rather than continuing as if it were unpaid.

docs.title: Change checklist
docs.text:
1. Update Credits if user-visible pricing changes.
  2. Keep billing.yaml and plan grants in sync.
  3. Ensure every catalog model resolves rates (OpenRouter or a yaml override).
  4. Keep every model call on the shared invoke path so charging cannot be skipped.

The next operator chapter is how to see those charges on a running job: Watching a job.

docs.title: Shipping to production
docs.text:
This chapter is for someone who needs a change to reach the live site. It answers what the release path is, why build and deploy are separate steps, and how to run them for this repository.

Three product repositories and one infra repository share a single VPS. Building images and deploying the stack are separate on purpose: a green build does not restart production by itself. That keeps a broken image from going live because a push happened to succeed, and it lets you build OCR and Query independently, then cut over together.

Infra setup (runners, keys, and the first-time VPS layout) belongs to the separate nolain-platform repository. This page documents the release flow after that infrastructure is available.

The picture, as a sequence rather than a graph:

  1. A push to nolain-ocr (branch master) or nolain-query (branch main / platform) builds Docker images on a self-hosted runner and pushes them to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry).
  2. Nothing happens on the VPS yet.
  3. Someone (or a push to nolain-platform) runs Deploy platform to VPS. That runner pulls the images and runs docker compose pull && up -d on the machine that actually serves traffic.

The rest of the chapter is what each component does, what you do after a code change, and what to check when the site is still old.

docs.title: 1. nolain-ocr — Build and push to GHCR
docs.text: What it does On push to master, builds backend and frontend Docker images on the VPS runner, pushes them to GHCR tagged :master, :latest, and :<git-sha>. Frontend build bakes in VITE_* values from GitHub secrets. Admin action required? One-time: GitHub secrets for every VITE_* the frontend Dockerfile expects. Per change: push to master (or Actions → Run workflow). Maintenance? Update nolain-ocr GitHub secrets when a new VITE_* build arg is added to the frontend, or when Supabase/Google/Stripe public IDs change.

docs.title: 2. nolain-query — Build and push to GHCR
docs.text: What it does On push to main / platform, builds cloud_api backend and nolainquery-website images on the Query self-hosted runner (~/actions-runner-query). Tags: :main or :platform, :latest, :<git-sha>. Website bakes in VITE_SUPABASE_* from secrets; VITE_CLOUD_API_URL=https://nolainquery.com. Admin action required? One-time: register third runner on VPS for nolain-query; set VITE_SUPABASE_URL, VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY secrets (same Supabase project as OCR). Per change: push branch → wait for build ✅ → run platform deploy. Maintenance? Grant nolain-platform GHCR read access to new Query packages (or extend GHCR_PAT). While testing Phase 2, platform compose uses :platform tags; switch to :main after merge.

docs.title: 3. nolain-platform — Deploy platform to VPS
docs.text: What it does On push to platform / main, or manual trigger: pulls latest platform repo on the VPS, logs into GHCR, runs docker compose pull && up -d using docker-compose.prod.yml and /opt/nolain/.env. Restarts nginx, OCR, Query, redis, celery workers. Reloads nginx config after up. Admin action required? One-time: GHCR_PAT secret on nolain-platform (read packages). Platform repo cloned on VPS with deploy key (Step 1.4 in guide). After product code changes: trigger this manually — it does not run when OCR or Query builds finish. Maintenance? Rotate GHCR_PAT before expiry. Update /opt/nolain/.env when backend runtime env vars change. Add Query keys (DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, QUERY_*) once (Phase 2).

docs.title: 4. Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners (×3)
docs.text: What it does Executes workflow jobs on the VPS. One runner per repo: nolain-ocr (builds), nolain-platform (deploy), nolain-query (builds). All need the vps label. Admin action required? One-time: install and register all three; keep systemd services running (actions-runner, actions-runner-platform, actions-runner-query). Query runner may run via ./run.sh until root installs svc.sh. Maintenance? Upgrade runner version occasionally. Restart service if jobs sit in Waiting for a runner… while the runner shows Idle.

docs.title: 5. GHCR (GitHub Container Registry)
docs.text: What it does Stores built images. Platform compose references OCR :master and Query :platform (or :main after merge). Admin action required? None for day-to-day — build workflows push; deploy workflow pulls. Maintenance? Ensure nolain-platform has package read access for Query images (403 → refresh GHCR_PAT or grant package access).

docs.title: 6. VPS runtime — Docker stack + /opt/nolain/.env
docs.text: What it does Runs production containers (8 services after Phase 2). Shared Supabase keys; OCR Stripe/Mistral keys; Query DEEPSEEK_API_KEY and QUERY_* quotas. Nginx routes nolainocr.com → OCR, nolainquery.com → Query (HTTP until SSL cert; see guide Step 2.3). Admin action required? Edit .env on the VPS when backend env vars change. Point DNS nolainquery.com → VPS IP; run certbot for HTTPS. Maintenance? Backup .env and certbot/. Add Supabase redirect URL for https://nolainquery.com/**.

docs.title: 7. Domains
docs.text:
Domain Routes to nolainocr.com OCR frontend + /api → OCR backend nolainquery.com Query website + /api → Query backend

Query uses HTTP on port 80 until Let's Encrypt cert exists for nolainquery.com (DNS must point to VPS first).
